topics.name: Comparing: Adjectives, Adverbs and as … as

steps.caption: To compare two things, short adjectives add -er + than. Long adjectives use more + adjective + than. Good and bad are irregular.
Big ends in one vowel and one consonant, so we double the g: big → bigger than. «My bag is bigger than yours.»
Long adjectives don't add -er. Use more + adjective + than: «This jumper is more colourful than that one.»
An adverb of manner tells us how we do something. Most are adjective + -ly: «She writes neatly.» Good → well and fast → fast are irregular: «He plays well. She runs fast.»
To compare how people do things, use more + adverb + than: «Ana writes more neatly than me.» Well → better and fast → faster: «Tom swims faster than Leo.»
as + adjective or adverb + as means the same (equal): «He's as tall as Krish.» «Max plays the guitar as well as Krish.»
not as + adjective + as means less: «Her new schoolbag is not as big as her old one.» «Ben isn't as brave as Frankie» means Frankie is braver than Ben.
Spelling rules. Adjectives that end in consonant + y change y to i and add -er: heavy → heavier, easy → easier. Adjectives that end in e add only -r: nice → nicer, large → larger.

Put much or a lot before a comparative to make the difference bigger: «The blue jacket is much more expensive than the grey jacket.» «This outfit is a lot more interesting than the others.» To say less, use isn't as … as: «My bag isn't as heavy as yours.»

steps.caption: We can use the present simple to talk about the future when it is a timetable or a schedule: «The bus leaves in five minutes.»
Buses, trains, flights, shows and classes happen at fixed times, so we use the present simple for them.

steps.caption: With he, she, it or one thing, add -s or -es to the verb: the show starts, the bus leaves, the party finishes. With plural subjects there is no -s: «The models arrive at ten.»
Questions use does or do + the base verb, with no -s: «What time does the flight leave? When does the party start? What days do they have parties?»

steps.caption: In the past, people used natural materials to make clothes: animal fur and skin, leaves and plants.
In the Middle Ages, most people wore warm woollen clothes. The wool came from sheep. Clothes and shoes were very simple, and shoes were made of leather.
Silk and colourful dyed clothes were very expensive, so only very rich people wore them. Dyes give clothes their colour.
Today we use natural materials and manmade materials. Manmade materials are cheaper.
Swimwear is made of manmade materials because they dry faster. Check the label on your clothes to see what they are made of.

Synthetic fleece can be made from recycled plastic bottles: about 25 bottles make one fleece jumper. It is warm and waterproof. But when we wash it, microplastics (tiny pieces of plastic) go into rivers and the sea and pollute them.
